reference.source: Miller's Review of Orthopaedics / Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Avulsion of the anteroinferior glenoid labrum (with the inferior glenohumeral ligament) after an anterior shoulder dislocation
A bony Bankart lesion involves an associated fracture of the anteroinferior glenoid rim and increases recurrence risk
It is the classic labral lesion of traumatic anterior instability and typically pairs with a Hill-Sachs impaction of the humeral head
Younger age at first dislocation is the strongest predictor of recurrent instability
Apprehension and relocation tests are positive; recurrent subluxation may cause activity-limiting apprehension rather than pain
Significant glenoid bone loss shifts management from soft-tissue repair towards bony augmentation (e.g. Latarjet-type procedures)
CT quantifies glenoid bone loss and MR arthrography best shows the soft-tissue labroligamentous injury
reference.pathophysiology: During traumatic anterior glenohumeral dislocation the humeral head levers against and strips the anteroinferior labrum and inferior glenohumeral ligament from the glenoid rim, sometimes taking a fragment of bone (bony Bankart). Loss of this labroligamentous bumper and of glenoid concavity reduces the barrier to anterior translation, predisposing to recurrent instability; concurrent posterolateral humeral head impaction (Hill-Sachs) can engage the glenoid rim and perpetuate dislocation.
additionalDifferentials: Hill-Sachs lesion and engaging bipolar bone loss
Glenoid rim fracture without labral avulsion
Rotator cuff tear (more common cause of instability in older patients)
additionalInvestigations: Radiographs including axillary and apical oblique views
MR arthrography to demonstrate the labroligamentous lesion
CT with glenoid bone-loss quantification (glenoid track assessment)
Examination under anaesthesia and diagnostic arthroscopy
redFlags: Neurovascular deficit after dislocation (axillary nerve or brachial plexus injury)
Inability to reduce the joint or locked dislocation
Large engaging bone loss indicating high re-dislocation risk with soft-tissue-only repair
reference.prognosis: Recurrence is common in young athletes managed non-operatively; arthroscopic or open stabilisation restores stability in most, with outcomes strongly dependent on the degree of glenoid and humeral bone loss.
pitfalls: Underestimating glenoid bone loss and performing a soft-tissue repair destined to fail
Overlooking an axillary nerve injury after dislocation
Missing associated rotator cuff tears in patients over 40 who dislocate
Ignoring bipolar (glenoid plus Hill-Sachs) bone loss and the glenoid track concept
management: Reduce the acute dislocation and immobilise briefly, followed by structured physiotherapy to restore rotator-cuff and scapular control
Offer arthroscopic Bankart repair with labroligamentous reattachment for recurrent instability, particularly in young athletes at high recurrence risk
Perform a bony augmentation procedure such as the Latarjet coracoid transfer when there is significant glenoid bone loss or an engaging Hill-Sachs lesion
Quantify glenoid and humeral bone loss with CT and glenoid-track assessment to guide the choice of soft-tissue versus bony reconstruction
Advise activity modification and avoidance of provocative abduction-external rotation positions while deciding on surgery
Rehabilitate progressively after stabilisation before graded return to sport
Refer to a shoulder or sports-orthopaedic surgeon for recurrent or bony instability
